summary: This RFC specifies the Reliable Data Protocol, which gives packet-based applications a reliable data transport service. It was a proposal, and the authors asked for discussion and suggestions. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: When you send ten postcards, you want to know all ten arrived in the right order. This protocol makes sure nothing is lost or mixed up.

subtitle: A small, connection-oriented transport for loading and debugging, with reliable delivery but optional ordering.

tldr.problem: Remote loading and debugging need every message delivered, efficiently, over lossy and slow networks, but TCP's byte stream and strict ordering add complexity and force needless retransmission.
tldr.mechanism: RDP is a connection-oriented protocol over IP that carries whole messages as segments, uses a three-way handshake, a 32-bit checksum, sequence numbers and acknowledgements, and can acknowledge out-of-order segments so only the missing one is resent.
tldr.outcome: RDP was published as an Experimental protocol that asked for discussion, and it was later updated by RFC 1151.

today: RFC 908 is an Experimental protocol specification that was updated by RFC 1151. It was published asking for discussion and suggestions rather than as a standard.

sections.title: Why Not Just Use TCP
sections.content:
The Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) is meant for packet-based applications such as remote loading and debugging. Its aim is to be simple to implement yet efficient where there are long transmission delays and where segments are lost or arrive out of order.

The RFC lists what such applications need. Delivery must be reliable, because a loaded memory image cannot have a hole in it. Data must move efficiently, so one lost segment should not force a resend of everything after it. Ordering is optional: loading and dumping do not need it, but a debugger may need to know a breakpoint command arrived before a proceed command is sent.

The authors say this made the design start to look like TCP, and explain why they did not choose it. TCP is built for a general byte stream, which is a source of complexity. It will not acknowledge a byte until all earlier bytes are acknowledged, which forces needless retransmission. It always delivers in order, which can tie up buffers. RDP supports a much simpler set of functions and can be subset further, for example a loader that only implements the passive Open and a single connection.
sections.eli5: TCP is a big truck built to carry anything. For simple jobs like loading a computer, a small van that does just what you need is easier to build and faster.

sections.title: Connections, Ports and States
sections.content:
RDP is connection-oriented and each connection is a full-duplex channel between two processes. Source and destination ports are 8 bits each and, together with the network addresses, identify a connection. Well-known ports are 1 to 63 and allocable ports are 64 to 255.

A connection starts with an Open request, either passive (listen for a remote request) or active (contact a specific remote host and port). The connection record moves through six states: CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RCVD, OPEN and CLOSE-WAIT. Each side picks an initial sequence number, and in the SYN segment tells the other its maximum segment size and the maximum number of unacknowledged segments it will hold. If two hosts open at the same moment, the crossing SYNs are handled by repeating the SYN with an ACK added.

Closing is simple. A Close request sends an RST segment and enters CLOSE-WAIT for a delay, discarding segments that arrive. Because of this, users must make sure all data was delivered before they close. A NUL segment can be used to check that a quiet connection is still valid, which helps find half-open connections after a crash.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two computers say hello, agree on a starting number and how much mail each can hold. To hang up, one says goodbye and waits a moment in case any stray mail is still arriving.

sections.title: Messages, Acknowledgements and Flow Control
sections.content:
Each user message sent with a Send request becomes a single RDP segment: an RDP header plus one or more octets of data. RDP does not split large messages or reassemble them. If a message is larger than the maximum segment size for the connection, the Send returns an error, and a received segment that is too large causes the connection to be aborted with an RST.

Reliability comes from sequence numbers, a checksum on every segment, positive acknowledgement and a retransmission timer for each segment. Sequence numbers start from a monotonically increasing clock and go up by one for each segment that carries data. A normal ACK is cumulative and names the last segment received in sequence. A segment that arrives out of sequence is acknowledged with an EACK that lists its sequence number, so the sender need only resend what is missing. Receivers may choose not to implement EACKs and senders may ignore them.

Flow control counts unacknowledged segments. Each side states its limit in the SYN and cannot change it for the life of the connection. The acceptance window starts just after the last in-sequence acknowledged number and extends for twice the allowed number of outstanding segments. Sequenced delivery is chosen when the connection is opened and holds for its whole life. Otherwise segments are handed to the user in arrival order.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a number and travels on its own. The receiver says which ones it got, even if they came out of order, so the sender only repeats the ones that went missing.

sections.title: The RDP Header and Segment Types
sections.content:
Every segment starts with an RDP header whose length can vary. The first octet holds the control flags (SYN, ACK, EACK, RST, NUL, plus one unused bit) and a 2-bit version number whose current value is 1. The next octet is the header length in units of two octets; a header with no variable part has the value 9.

After that come 8-bit source and destination ports, a 16-bit data length, a 32-bit sequence number, a 32-bit acknowledgement number and a 32-bit checksum. The checksum covers header and data. It is a non-linear algorithm: add each 32-bit word into an accumulator, ignore any carry out, then rotate the accumulator left one bit, treating the checksum field as zero and padding a short last word with zeros.

The segment types are variations on this header. SYN adds the maximum number of outstanding segments, the maximum segment size and an options field whose first bit, SDM, selects sequenced delivery. ACK acknowledges in-sequence data and can carry data. EACK adds a list of out-of-sequence sequence numbers received. RST closes or resets, and NUL probes whether the other side is still active. SYN, RST and NUL never carry user data. Over IP, RDP uses the version 4 IP header; the RFC leaves the protocol number as ???.
sections.eli5: Each message has a label on the front saying who it is from, who it is for, how long it is and a number to spot damage. Small special messages say hello, goodbye, got it, or are you still there.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC closes with example exchanges. In a normal open, Host A sends SEQ=100 SYN to a listening Host B, which replies SEQ=200 ACK=100 SYN,ACK. Host A then answers with SEQ=101 ACK=200 and both sides are in OPEN.

In the lost-segment example, segment 101 is lost while 102 and 103 arrive. Host B acknowledges those with EA=102 and EA=102,103, and after Host A resends only 101, B acknowledges up to 103. The out-of-order and long-delay examples show that a sender need not wait for an acknowledgement before sending more, up to the allowed number of unacknowledged segments (five in one example). Two more examples show how a host that crashed and restarted discovers a half-open connection and resets the other side.

An appendix describes implementing a minimal RDP.
sections.eli5: The examples show the game in action: a missing postcard is noticed, and only that one is sent again instead of the whole stack.
